A.3 Theorem 3 (simulation) Let A be row-stochastic and set B = A/n. Then B 1 = 1/n and B⊤ 1 ≤ 1, so every row and column sum of B is at most one. By the doubly stochastic extension theorem [7] there is a doubly stochastic matrix Q of order 2n with Qij = Bij for i, j ≤ n. Therefore n   Q[1:n,1:n] V = A V, and the scalar n is absorbed into WO. □ Proposition 1 (dustbin). Let A be any row-stochastic matrix and b = A⊤ 1. Then A ∈ U(1, b), and U(1, b) is the feasible set of a balanced layer in which the column marginal is free. Hence the null-column variant contains every softmax attention pattern as a feasible point, and its optimum coincides with softmax attention in the limit where the null column absorbs the entire column defect. The first claim is a direct computation; the second follows from the standard equivalence between unbalanced transport with a free marginal and balanced transport with a dustbin [8]. □

A.4 Note on the gradient The claim in Section 4.4 follows from the envelope theorem applied to F(C) = minP ∈ U(1,1) ⟨ P, C ⟩ - ε H(P), which is a minimum of affine functions of C and therefore concave in C; its gradient is P*, so ∂ P*/∂ C is symmetric and negative semidefinite with spectrum bounded by the entropy scale. The bound is tight in the uniform-plan limit, where P* does not depend on C at all.

C Distractor probe We concatenate a short sentiment sentence with k unrelated news paragraphs and fine-tune the 1.4B models for 2B tokens on the task. With k = 8, uniform marginals reach 88.4% accuracy, the null-column variant 91.2%, and the softmax baseline 90.6%. The result is the expected one: when the correct behaviour is to ignore most of the input, the ability to dump mass is worth having, and it is worth having as an option rather than as the only behaviour.
